opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. In practice, I think open source means a few different things, and people often mix them up.

The first layer is the most literal one: the code is out there, and anyone can read it, use it, and modify it. That's important, but honestly it's the least interesting part. Putting code on GitHub doesn't by itself make something a successful open source project.

The second layer, and the one I care about more, is that open source is a way of building things together. When I wrote Caffe back in grad school, it started as something I needed for my own research. What made it matter wasn't that the code was public; it was that other people started using it, filing issues, sending pull requests, writing tutorials, building models on top of it. The project became bigger than me. Later, working on Caffe2 and then on PyTorch, you saw the same thing at a much larger scale. The value comes from the community, not just the repository.

The third layer is that open source is a kind of standardization mechanism. In AI especially, a lot of the infrastructure, frameworks, model formats, even models themselves, becomes a common language. When everyone builds on the same foundation, the whole field moves faster because people stop reinventing the basic plumbing and focus on the actual new ideas.

And then there's the practical, business side, which I think people sometimes are a bit naive about. Open source isn't charity. Companies open source things because it helps them attract developers, set standards, build an ecosystem, or commoditize a layer so they can compete on another layer. That's not a bad thing, it's just reality. The healthiest projects are the ones where the incentives of the company and the community are aligned.

So if I had to sum it up: open source in practice is less about the license and more about whether you've built something people want to collaborate on, and whether there's a sustainable reason for everyone involved to keep investing in it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think a lot of people hear "open source" and picture a license file and a GitHub repo, and that's really just the starting point. For me, open source in practice is about three things, and the code is honestly the least interesting of them.

The first is lowering the barrier to entry. When I wrote Caffe back at Berkeley, the point wasn't that the code was especially clever. The point was that a grad student with a single GPU could download it, run a reference model in an afternoon, and start asking their own research questions instead of spending three months reimplementing AlexNet. That compounding effect, where thousands of people skip the same three months, is the real value.

The second is building a shared language. When a model architecture or a file format or a set of benchmarks becomes open, it becomes something everyone can point at and say, "this is what we mean." That's how a field converges. Without it, every lab and every company speaks its own dialect, and you lose enormous effort in translation.

The third, and this is the part people underestimate, is trust and feedback. If you ship something closed, you get a support queue. If you ship something open, you get people who read your code, find your bugs, and sometimes tell you your design was wrong before you've invested another year in it. That's painful but incredibly healthy. Some of the best contributors to PyTorch and ONNX were people who showed up because they were frustrated with something and decided to fix it.

Now, the honest caveat: open source is not free. Maintaining a project well is a real job. Reviewing pull requests, keeping documentation current, deciding what not to merge, all of that takes people and money. Companies that treat open source as marketing and then disappear tend to leave projects stranded. So "open source in practice" also means being clear about who is paying for the maintenance and why they'll keep doing it. If that answer is solid, the project tends to live. If it isn't, it usually fades no matter how good the initial code was.

astra-6.text:
I think open source is fundamentally a way of collaborating. Making your code available is one part of it, but the more interesting part is what happens afterward: Can someone understand it, use it, change it, and contribute something back?

For example, you might build a tool to solve a problem you have. Once you open-source it, somebody else tries it in an environment you never considered. They discover a limitation, or they find a new use for it. If you make it easy for those people to participate, the project can become much more useful than what you could have built alone.

That also means open source takes work. You need documentation, you need to respond to issues, and you need to explain why you accept some changes and reject others. Publishing a repository is a starting point. Building trust and a community around it is what makes that collaboration sustainable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think open source is fundamentally a way of collaborating. Making the code public is the starting point: people can see how something works, use it, and modify it for their own needs. But the real value comes when they can contribute what they learn back to the project.

In practice, that takes more than putting a repository online. You need documentation, a clear license, and a process for discussing problems and reviewing contributions. You also have to be willing to listen, because someone using your software may discover a use case you never anticipated.

So I would distinguish between publishing code and building an open-source community. Publishing code makes knowledge available. Building a community allows that knowledge to keep growing beyond the original authors.
